title: U.S. Senate · Nebraska

context.text: Cindy Burbank, who won the May 12, 2026 Democratic primary, filed paperwork to withdraw from the general election on July 17, 2026, saying, "I've looked at the numbers. I won't be your next senator. So I have withdrawn my bid for U.S. Senate." She is not listed below and does not appear on the general-election ballot.
Incumbent Pete Ricketts was appointed to the U.S. Senate in January 2023 to fill the vacancy left by Ben Sasse, then won a special election in November 2024 to serve the remainder of that term.

summary.text: Pete Ricketts is the Republican incumbent U.S. Senator from Nebraska. He worked for the brokerage firm that became Ameritrade, ran unsuccessfully for the Senate in 2006, and served as Governor of Nebraska from 2015 to 2023 before being appointed to the Senate in January 2023. He won the 2024 special election for the seat and is now seeking election again; according to Ballotpedia's summary of his campaign website, he campaigns on tax cuts, border security and reducing federal spending.

background.text: Born August 19, 1964, in Nebraska City and raised in Omaha, the son of an entrepreneur and a school teacher; graduated from Westside High School.
Earned a bachelor's degree in biology (1986) and an MBA in marketing and finance (1991) from the University of Chicago.

Worked for Union Pacific, then joined his family's business, which became Ameritrade, in 1993; his roles there included senior vice president of strategy and business development, senior vice president of marketing, president and chief operating officer.

Founded Drakon LLC, which supports Nebraska entrepreneurs and startup companies, and was a past board member of TD Ameritrade and the Chicago Cubs; he and three siblings purchased the Cubs and Wrigley Field in 2009.

Left Ameritrade in 2006 to run for the U.S. Senate; he won the Republican primary and lost the general election to incumbent Democrat Ben Nelson. In 2007 he co-founded the Platte Institute for Economic Research.

Served as Nebraska's 40th Governor, sworn in January 8, 2015, and re-elected in November 2018, succeeding Dave Heineman and succeeded by Jim Pillen. His Senate biography says he worked with the Legislature on more than $12.7 billion in tax relief and cut the growth of state spending.

Appointed to the U.S. Senate in January 2023 to fill the vacancy created by Ben Sasse's resignation and sworn in on January 23, 2023; won the November 2024 special general election over Preston Love Jr. (D), 62.6% to 37.4%.
Serves on the Senate Environment and Public Works, Foreign Relations, Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and Budget committees.

According to his Senate biography, he serves on the board of the Mid-America Council of the Boy Scouts and as a director of the Nebraska Game and Parks Foundation, and lives in Omaha with his wife, Susanne Shore; they have three children.

priorities.text: Cutting taxes, citing the 2025 federal reconciliation bill's tax cuts and his record of state tax cuts as governor.
Border security, citing votes for border-security funding and hiring additional Border Patrol agents.
"Making government work better" by reducing federal spending and waste, including as a member of the DOGE Caucus.
National security, citing his role on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and votes for defense funding, including for Offutt Air Force Base and the Sentinel ICBM program.

positions.summary: Cosponsored S. 128, the SAVE Act, which requires documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.
Cosponsored S. 9, the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act of 2025, which would bar transgender women and girls from women's and girls' school sports.

His Senate issues page says that as governor he signed legislation ending dismemberment abortion, and that as a Pro-Life Caucus member he supports legislation to ban federal taxpayer funding of abortion and to protect babies who survive abortion attempts.
His Senate issues page says he is pushing back on emissions mandates that would force a mass transition to electric vehicles and supports an all-of-the-above energy mix.
positions.quote: emissions mandates that would force a mass transition to electric vehicles

record.text: Serves on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works (chairing the Subcommittee on Fisheries, Wildlife, and Water), the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and the Committee on Foreign Relations, in the 119th Congress (2025-2026).
Says he introduced the bipartisan Improper Payments Transparency Act aimed at reducing federal waste and improper payments.
Says he introduced bipartisan legislation to limit foreign adversaries', including China's, ability to own U.S. farmland.
As Governor of Nebraska (2015-2023), says he delivered $12.7 billion in state tax relief, including ending state taxes on Social Security and military retirement benefits.

summary.text: Dan Osborn is an industrial mechanic and union leader from Omaha running as an independent (ballot line "Nonpartisan") for the second consecutive Senate cycle. A Navy and Nebraska Army National Guard veteran who led the 2021 Kellogg's strike, he lost to Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024. His campaign centers on congressional ethics reform, consumer-protection and antitrust measures, and opposition to cuts in Social Security and Medicare.

background.text: Born March 29, 1975; his family moved to Omaha when he was seven, and he graduated from Roncalli Catholic High School in 1994. He lives in Omaha.
Enlisted in the U.S. Navy after high school, serving four years as a storekeeper aboard the USS Constellation (CV-64), and later served in the Nebraska Army National Guard.

Began work in 2004 as an industrial mechanic at the Kellogg's plant in Omaha, where he became president of Local 50G of the Bakery, Confectionery, Tobacco Workers, and Grain Millers International Union.

Led the 2021 Kellogg's strike, which was prompted by a two-tier pay system and lasted 77 days; he later worked in boiler maintenance and repair at Boys Town and joined Steamfitters and Plumbers Local 464.
Announced a 2024 independent campaign for U.S. Senate on October 5, 2023, and lost to incumbent Sen. Deb Fischer (R) 53.2% to 46.5%. He has been registered as nonpartisan since 2004.

In 2026 he is again running as an independent against Sen. Ricketts; he submitted about 12,500 signatures on June 11, 2026, to qualify for the ballot. The Nebraska Democratic Party has endorsed his candidacy, and he has said he would not caucus with either major party.

priorities.text: Anti-corruption reform: overturning Citizens United, banning congressional stock trading, closing the lobbying "revolving door," and enacting term and age limits for Congress and the courts.
Protecting paychecks, Social Security and healthcare, including opposing benefit cuts and raising the Social Security payroll-tax cap on high earners.
Cutting government waste and fraud and balancing the federal budget without cutting Social Security or Medicare benefits.
Consumer-protection measures such as click-to-cancel subscription rules, reining in credit-card swipe fees, and right-to-repair laws.

positions.summary: Supports raising or eliminating the income cap on Social Security payroll taxes so high earners pay the same rate as other workers.
positions.quote: Right now, millionaires and billionaires stop paying into Social Security after their first $176,100 in income... Raising or eliminating that cap so the wealthy pay the same rate as everyone else would extend Social Security's solvency for decades without cutting a single benefit for a single retiree.

positions.summary: Says he supports the Second Amendment right to bear arms while also backing gun-safety education in schools.
positions.quote: I am fundamentally in favor of the Second Amendment. While I support reasonable safety measures, including gun safety education in our schools, law-abiding citizens have, and must always have, the right to bear arms.

positions.summary: Says he is personally pro-life but that abortion and other medical decisions should remain between a patient and their doctor, not the government.
positions.quote: I am personally pro-life, but believe the government should not be making health decisions for people. It is important that people have the right to make their own choices in consultations with their doctors.

positions.summary: Opposes broad, across-the-board tariffs, saying he supports only narrow, targeted tariffs.
positions.quote: Blanket tariffs raise everyday costs for small businesses and families like mine... I support a smart, America-first tariff policy. Targeted. Strategic.

positions.summary: Supports letting Medicaid negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers, as the VA does, and opposes Medicaid cuts affecting rural hospitals.
positions.quote: I support giving Medicaid the full authority to negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers, the same way the VA does, the same way every other wealthy country does.

candidates.name: Mike Marvin

summary.text: Mike Marvin won the Legal Marijuana Now Party primary and is on the Nov. 3, 2026 general-election ballot for U.S. Senate. His campaign website states that, citing worsening health, he cannot put in the effort the race requires, will remain on the ballot, and urges supporters to back Dan Osborn.

background.text: Earned a high school diploma from Dominican High School.
Career experience includes serving as executive director of the Nebraska Association of Public Employees (described by Ballotpedia as a former role).

priorities.text: Legalizing marijuana nationally for medical and recreational purposes.
Repealing the PATRIOT Act and ending government surveillance of citizens.
Ending the Supreme Court's Citizens United ruling and funding elections with tax dollars.
Protecting Social Security (eliminating its income cap) and expanding Medicare and Medicaid.

positions.summary: On his campaign website (April 29, 2026), said Medicare and Medicaid must be expanded to eventually cover every American.
positions.quote: Medicare and Medicaid must be expanded, and eventually cover every single American.

candidates.researchNotes: Positions are from the campaign website text of April 29, 2026 as quoted verbatim by Ballotpedia. His campaign site now states that, citing worsening health, he cannot put in the effort the race requires, will remain on the ballot, and urges supporters to back Dan Osborn. Has not completed the Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey. Only one position squarely matched the guide's issues.

candidates.name: Chuck Conboy

summary.text: Chuck Conboy is running on the America First Party Nebraska line in the Nov. 3, 2026 general election for U.S. Senate. He works in flooring and cabinet sales.

priorities.text: Opposes U.S. involvement in the conflict in Iran, arguing the money should stay in the country, per Nebraska Public Media.

positions.summary: Told Nebraska Public Media he supports the America First Party position of deporting people in the country illegally.
positions.quote: They want to deport all illegal aliens, which, I'm for that.

candidates.researchNotes: His campaign site (conboyforsenate.com) had no issue content in the text we could load. Immigration and Iran statements are from Nebraska Public Media's voter guide, which also reports his opposition to abortion without a direct quote, so no abortion stance was added. No Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey found. The America First Party nominee was named on Sept. 1, 2026.

candidates.name: Robin Richards

summary.text: Robin Richards is running on the Nebraska Working People Party line in the Nov. 3, 2026 general election for U.S. Senate. She chairs the party.

background.text: Born in David City, Nebraska; earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Nebraska Omaha in 2015 and attended Colorado State University (2018) and Cornell University (2021).

In a Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey response, describes herself as a Ralston graduate who works as business manager and accountant for the Nebraska Arts Council and as the state's Accessibility Coordinator through the National Endowment for the Arts.
Won an at-large seat on the Ralston Public Schools board in the November 5, 2024 general election and, per her survey response, serves as its vice president.
Ran for Nebraska State Senate District 12 in 2022 and lost the general election; in 2026 she also ran as a write-in in the May 12 primary for the same district and lost.

priorities.text: Said she wants expanded and protected disability services, particularly for children and in rural areas, per Nebraska Public Media.
Said she supports ensuring Social Security is solvent and not taxed, and child tax credits, per Nebraska Public Media.

candidates.researchNotes: Priorities are from Nebraska Public Media's voter guide (paraphrase, no stance on the guide's issue statements). No 2026 campaign website or Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey found; her only Ballotpedia survey (2022) was for a different office and is not used.
